Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The Climate Change Bill 2022 would write Australia's emissions reduction targets into domestic law.

It would require the minister to give an annual statement to Parliament on progress towards the targets and oblige the Climate Change Authority to provide advice on new or updated targets at least every five years.
The first independent review of the bill's operation must occur within five years, with subsequent reviews every ten years.
Sets emissions reduction targets in domestic legislation.
Requires an annual climate change statement to Parliament by the minister.
Mandates the Climate Change Authority to advise on targets every five years.
Requires the minister to explain in writing and table reasons if not accepting the authority's advice.
Provides for periodic independent reviews every ten years after the first within five years.
The Australian community, Parliament, the minister, the Climate Change Authority, and government agencies delivering programs contributing to emissions reduction.

Climate Change Bill 2022, Climate Change (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2022 - Third Reading - Pass the bills

The Climate Change (Consequential Amendments) Bill embeds Australia's greenhouse gas emissions reduction targets into the functions of entities including the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, ARENA, CSIRO, Infrastructure Australia, the Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility, and Export Finance Australia, and updates references to the Paris Agreement.

A motion was moved to suspend standing orders to allow a flexible debate schedule for the Climate Change Bill 2022, including 10-minute speaking times, a possible reduction to 5 minutes after 9pm, and a minister’s discretion to adjourn after 10pm. The mover argued the approach maximises participation and contrasts with the previous government's restriction of debate, noting that all speakers were heard during recent proceedings ending at 10pm.

The government abandoned its election promise to cut household power bills by $275, legislating only a 43% emissions reduction target without any price protections, while the bill's consequential amendments risk enabling green lawfare and restricting agencies like Export Finance Australia, Infrastructure Australia and the Northern Australia Infrastructure Fund.

The speaker defended the Climate Change Bill 2022, arguing it implements Labor’s election policy of a 43% emissions reduction by 2030, 82% renewable energy by 2030, and lower energy prices by 2025, while criticising the member for Fairfax for ignoring facts and accusing the former government of hiding a report on rising energy prices.

The speaker welcomed the Climate Change Bill 2022 as progress but argued it is not comprehensive, lacking mechanisms, risk assessments, adaptation plans, and a ratchet mechanism, and criticised the 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 as politically rather than scientifically motivated, urging greater ambition and no new fossil fuel projects.

The speaker supported the Climate Change Bill 2022, which sets a 43% emissions reduction target by 2030, despite preferring a 50% target, and cited recent bushfires and floods costing over $8 billion to argue for urgent climate action.

The speaker argued the Climate Change Bill 2022 and related amendments are vital for Australia, establishing emissions reduction targets, accountability mechanisms, and independent expert advice. They announced the Albanese Labor government's policies include Rewiring the Nation, community battery investments, electric vehicle tax reductions, a safeguard mechanism for major polluters, and $45 million in ARENA funding for the University of New South Wales' solar research.

The speaker argued the Climate Change Bill 2022 is a historic step but requires stronger accountability, noting it enshrines a 43% emissions reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050, while criticising gaps such as a missing target review mechanism, no consequences for non-compliance, and failure to extend targets to the EPBC Act and Industry Research and Development Act.

The MP supported the Climate Change Bill 2022 and Climate Change (Consequential Amendments) Bill 2022, which legislate Australia's emissions targets of a 43 per cent reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050, and embed those targets across agencies including the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, ARENA, Export Finance Australia, Infrastructure Australia and the CSIRO. The MP also highlighted the Labor government's Powering Australia plan, which they said would deliver 604,000 jobs, and cited the delayed Star of the South project as a missed opportunity under the previous government.

The independent MP for North Sydney supported the Climate Change Bill as a foundational step but argued for stronger action, including a 60 per cent emissions reduction target by 2030, an end to fossil fuel subsidies, no new coal and gas projects, and mandatory fuel efficiency standards, noting that 96 per cent of consulted constituents backed the legislation.

The Climate Change Bill 2022 commits Australia to a 43% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions from 2005 levels by 2030 and net zero by 2050, backed by the Powering Australia plan targeting 82% renewable energy and 604,000 jobs. The bill also includes community battery installations for up to 100,000 households, electric vehicle tax exemptions, and a national electric vehicle strategy.

The member for Wentworth announced support for the Climate Change Bill 2022 but argued its 43% reduction target by 2030 is inadequate, advocating for at least 50% and calling for sector-specific policies, transparency on fossil fuel subsidies, and stronger accountability mechanisms.

The MP argued that the Climate Change Bill 2022 must pass to end a decade of inaction, set a 43% emissions reduction target as a floor, and implement the Powering Australia plan—including community batteries like the one pledged for Belfield, a $3 billion National Reconstruction Fund for renewables and low‑emissions technology, and electric vehicle uptake—to create 604,000 new jobs and spur $76 billion in investment, while urging the opposition to drop nuclear distractions.

The speaker argued that the Climate Change Bill 2022, by adopting Greens policy, risks national security in the Pacific, restricts Infrastructure Australia and the Northern Australia Infrastructure Facility, and could hinder critical minerals processing and clean energy development. The speaker also claimed the bill lacks economic and equity safeguards, and that Labor broke its promise to reduce power bills by $275, while noting the coalition previously reduced emissions by over 20% below 2005 levels and cut power prices by 8% for households.

The government announced the Climate Change Bill will unlock up to $131 billion in energy investment, and argued that renewables are the cheapest and fastest energy option, rejecting nuclear as too expensive and slow to deploy, citing CSIRO GenCost 2021-22 findings.

The Climate Change Bill 2022 was defended, citing its legislated 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 (modelled by RepuTex), enshrining of net-zero pathways in ARENA, the CEFC, and the NAIF, and reinvestment in the Climate Change Authority. The speech also highlighted policies for over 80 solar banks and 400 community batteries, plus the $20 billion Sun Cable project in the Northern Territory.

The speaker supported the Climate Change Bill 2022 and related bills, arguing the Albanese government’s 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 and restoration of the Climate Change Authority are necessary steps after a decade of inaction, and that the legislation provides democratic legitimacy and accountability.

The speaker argued that the 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 should be a floor, not a ceiling, and that the government should exceed it, ideally reaching 60%. They also called for legislated emissions budgets through 2050 and a climate trigger in the EPBC Act to prevent new fossil fuel projects from undermining net zero.

The Albanese Labor government introduced the Climate Change Bill 2022, committing to a 43% emissions reduction by 2030 and net zero by 2050, with annual accountability statements and investments in renewable energy and solar batteries to lower costs and create jobs.

The speaker argued that legislating a 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 is a bad idea, despite supporting the target itself, citing risks of locking Australia into inflexible commitments while major emitters like China and India continue increasing emissions. They highlighted Australia's past success in exceeding emissions targets, criticized international carbon accounting methods as biased against resource-exporting nations, and warned that legislated targets could be used by activists to block new projects and harm industries like aluminium, steel, and fertiliser production.

The Albanese Labor government's Climate Change Bill 2022 legislates Australia's 2030 and 2050 emission reduction targets, requiring annual accountability statements and independent advice from the Climate Change Authority. The accompanying Consequential Amendments Bill integrates these targets into the objectives of agencies including the Clean Energy Finance Corporation, Australian Renewable Energy Agency, Export Finance Australia, Infrastructure Australia and CSIRO.

The MP supported the Climate Change Bill 2022 as a first step but argued its 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 is insufficient, calling for at least a 60–75% reduction and opposing new coal and gas projects. They committed to supporting the bill while vowing to continue pressing for more ambitious targets and further legislation.

The Climate Change Bill 2022 and related amendments are essential to end a decade of inaction, provide investment certainty for renewables, and honour the government's election commitment; the speaker supported a 43% emissions reduction target as an initial step and criticised past political games, including the Abbott opposition and the former prime minister brandishing coal in Parliament.

The speaker supported the Climate Change Bills 2022, arguing that Australia can end the climate wars and achieve a 43% emissions reduction by 2030 and net-zero by 2050, backed by a plan creating over 600,000 jobs and $76 billion in investment.
